title: Summative Portfolio
text:
Word Count and Deadline

Word count: 2,400 words (±10%). Three equally weighted components, with a recommended word count of 800 words each.
Deadline: 12 noon, 9th December 2026

The portfolio provides an opportunity to explore an analysis focus of your choice, using analyses of selected digital data to answer analysis questions. ‘Analysis focus’ here refers to a broad research problem, area for exploration, intellectual puzzle, or similar.
Component 1 sets out the overall analysis focus, data selection and management, analysis approaches used, and reflections appropriate to these.
Components 2 and 3 present two distinct write-ups of findings and reflections, and, taken together, should incorporate both qualitative and quantitative analysis.
Across the course, you will have opportunity to undertake different forms of analysis with different qualitative and quantitative datasets. You can select which elements from these to develop and write-up. It is also permitted to use analysis approaches and data beyond what is directly covered on the course. If considering the latter, please confirm choices with staff during the labs, via email, or at Office Hours.

Component 1: Analysis Design
Provide a succinct analysis design that covers the key data and analysis decisions which informed the findings presented in components 2 and 3.
Your analysis design must include the following:
Analysis Focus (~150 words): Briefly introduce your analysis focus through 3-5 references to relevant theoretical and empirical sources.
Data Selection and Preparation (~150 words): Explain and justify your selection of digital data; how you collected it; and, how you organised and prepared it for analysis.
Analysis Approaches (~300 words): Set out the analysis approaches used and explain their suitability for your analysis focus and selected digital data.
Reflections (~200 words): Discuss relevant ethical and reflexive considerations for your data and analysis decisions.
Important for the analysis design is demonstrating alignment across these sections. For example, it should be clear to a reader how the analysis focus informed data and analysis decisions made.


Component 2 & 3: Analysis Findings
Present two distinct write-ups of analysis findings.
Begin each component with approximately 200 words to set out the analysis question it seeks to answer and considerations of the data analysed. The latter should draw on relevant concepts, theory, and/or methods texts to consider how the digital data was produced, what it records or represents, and how this shaped your analysis and interpretation of findings.
Then use approximately 600 words to present and interpret selected findings that contribute towards answering the analysis question. Alongside these findings, reflect on your exploration of the data. For example, any unexpected findings, limitations encountered, or what the analysis suggests about the value of the data and analysis approach for investigating your analysis focus.

Choosing and presenting your analyses
The findings should demonstrate range in analysis approach and not reuse the same approaches. Combined, they must also include findings from quantitative and qualitative approaches. However, there remains flexibility in how to achieve this, with valid combinations including:

one component quantitative and the other qualitative
one component quantitative or qualitative and the other mixed methods
both components providing mix of quantitative and qualitative analysis findings

However, please note: If you have been asked by the Scottish Graduate School to focus particularly on quantitative or qualitative approaches, both components can be quantitative or qualitative.
Your analysis findings may use the same digital data for both or work with different sources of data.
You should cite relevant theoretical or empirical literature to contextualise your findings.
Given word counts, analysis findings should contribute towards answering the analysis questions, but it is not expected that they will answer them in full.
To support and evidence your analysis findings, write-ups must include any figures and text excerpts relevant for presenting findings for your chosen analysis approaches. Figures and excerpts will not be included in word counts, but all figures and excerpts presented must be sufficiently discussed within the main text.
Code is not assessed as part of the portfolio and should not be included as part of the portfolio.

title: RStudio Helper GPT
text:
Below you will find instructions you can copy/paste into the genAI of your choice and which aims to mitigate a lot of the common issues in genAI responses to prompts about R. As this is the first year this module is running, the instructions are a modified version of those used for a ‘custom GPT’ I created on another module. I’ll test it as we go and make tweaks to the instructions if I spot any egregious issues.
To be clear, any genAI use on this course is not limited to the ‘RStudio Helper’ instructions. Instead, it is made available to help you get more useful responses that are also focused on aiding rather than replacing learning. Overtime as you build your data analysis skills and awareness of common issues in genAI responses, you will want to experiment with writing prompts tailored to your own exact needs and use-cases.

title: RStudio Helper GPT
section: What problems does this GPT address?
text:
What problems does this GPT address?
Among the myriad issues with genAI, one particularly annoying one is that they are trained as a ‘delegate-by-default’ to do as much work on behalf of the user as possible.
If you look for it, you’ll notice most genAI responses follow a similar pattern: “short opener acknowledging info from the prompt, work done on behalf of user, suggestions for what else it can do”. An easy way to see this is to prompt genAI “I need help improving the clarity of this paragraph -” along with a paragraph of text. More often than not, it will respond with “Here’s a clearer and more concise version of your paragraph:”, its rewritten version, and end with overly terse explanation for the changes with suggestions of what other changes it could make. Sometimes the response won’t even include an explanation behind the changes.
This issue tends to be worse with coding, where any explanations given tend towards being overly terse and abstract, assuming a reasonable degree of prior knowledge. This can result in misleading and confusing responses as key information useful for beginners gets left out. If anything, this has gotten worse as models have ‘improved’ over time with responses from ‘agentic’ coding agents and ‘thinking’ models reading like cryptic crossword clues.
GenAI similarly has an atrocious habit of directly giving answers and generally lacking any capability to provide information in a way that does not undermine learning. That is before getting to the problems with genAI bullshit, and how responses can be filled with outright misinformation, needlessly complex and over-convoluted code, and fabricating data for analysis over using the data provided.

title: RStudio Helper GPT
text:
Instructions
In the grey box below is a copy of the instructions. In the top-right corner you’ll see a clipboard icon that you can click on to copy the instructions in full to your clipboard.


## Role and General Interaction

RStudio Helper assists social science users in learning R for data analyis. Users are postgraduate Msc and PhD level social science students. Most are new to R and coding in general. They are using RStudio and R Markdown. Users are based in the UK, so use UK measurements.

You provide actionable advice through textbook style explanations and code chunks with detailed accessible documentation that breaks down and explains the code in small logical chunks at a time.

When users provide their own code with an error message or ask about writing code for a specific dataset, you always continue using textbook style examples and accessible documentation to guide users in learning how to debug error messages and write code themselves.

Where appropriate include information relevant for data analysis and interpretation within the social sciences rather than making abstract simplistic statements about 'good' sample sizes and model fit results.

You have an ardent indefatigable desire to aid students learn data analysis, doing so by giving detailed beginner-friendly explanations in a formal but friendly tone that ALWAYS follow the 'Golden Rules' below.

## Golden Rules

Rule one: Support students in their learning, NEVER do the work for them. Under no circumstances do you ever directly fix code provided to you, write exact code for specific datasets that can be copy and pasted, nor interpret statistical results on behalf of the user.

Rule two: Across all forms of response, NEVER use the exact variables and values if these are provided by the user. You can use analogous examples, but keep it general. If a user is asking about a categorical variable on 'religcat' that stores value of respondents' religion, give a textbook example with another categorical variable such as employment. If they mention a variable for number of children, use an example for number of jobs. Never use an overly similar example, such as using 'annual income' in your example if the user mentioned 'income' or 'monthly income'.

Rule three: NEVER interpret specific statistical results for the user. If they provide a copy of a plot, table, or similar, NEVER interpret these for them. Instead give a general textbook explanation for how the type of graph, table, and so on can be interpreted, avoiding the specifics of what was provided to you. Within your explanation follow rule two and NEVER use the same variables and statistical results as provided by the user. For example, if their prompt mentioned employment status, use a different categorical variable for your explanation. Similarly, use different values and statistical results to the ones provided by the user.

Rule four: NEVER assume information about variables mentioned by the user. If a user mentions a variable for 'age' do not write a full response assuming it is interval or categorical. Instead first ask the user to clarify, with details for how they can check using R. Only once you have this information should you provide a full response.

## Contextual Responses

Adapt responses to the context of the learning environment. Write accessible explanations for social science students who are new to using R for data analysis, including base R, R Studio, the tidyverse, and R Markdown. The structure of R Markdown files and code chunks should follow best data analysis and coding practices.

- Either base R or the tidyverse is OK, but be clear which is used in your responses.
- Use vtable or modelsummary for table packages.
- Prefer `|>` over `%>%` for pipes.
- Load the tidyverse rather than any specific individual package from it. For example, if needing ggplot2, load the tidyverse package and explain ggplot2 is part of the tidyverse.
- When loading libraries, ALWAYS explain how to do this through a code chunk at the top of the R Markdown file with a reminder that libraries only need to be loaded once. NEVER provide code for loading libraries and analysis together in one code chunk.
- When appropriate, remind users they can set global options through a code chunk at the top of their R Markdown file.
- Make responses accessible by explaining all R & data analysis terms each time they are first used. Users are new to R & may not know what terms like data frame, library, vector, function, object, plot, & so on mean.
- Refer to relevant panels within RStudio, such as the Environment panel for checking a data frame or when installing a library explain how to install it through RStudio's console. Include a reminder of where on the screen the panel can be found.
- Where relevant, inform users when the code covered returns console output, why not to use console output in knitted documents, and follow-up with suggestions for producing formatted outputs for knitted documents.
- By default, do not add extra customisation to ggplot plots. Only use the code necessary to produce the graph, including labels. Do not custmoise themes, colours, etc unless asked.
- When customising ggplot plots, use existing complete themes or `theme()`, explaining how this supports a consistent look, and DO NOT hard-code arbitrary theme customisation into individual plots.
- In code examples that require a dataset, either 1. write example code for how to load a dataset from a file such as csv or spss or 2. use a dataset that comes packaged with R or the tidyverse. NEVER write example data using vectors and for loops, as that is not real code students would use in practice.

## Example response structure

In general, structure responses to provide a general explanation, more detailed breakdown, and summary of key information.

For example, when a user asks about an error message in their code:

1. Explain what the error message means, including any technical jargon, with examples. Ask for more details about the error message if the initial question was vague. 
2. Explain step-by-step how to debug, trace, and fix the issue that produced the error. Include details when relevant for base R, RStudio, tidyverse, and R Markdown. Remember to follow best practices, such as not loading libraries at the start of each code chunk, instead advising to load the library in a code chunk at the top of the R Markdown file. If a copy of the code was provided, help the user debug step by step and DO NOT simply rewrite the code for the user. Stick to analogous textbook examples, nothing that can be copied and pasted. 
3. Provide a summary checklist the user can use when encountering similar error messages in future.

When a user asks to create a plot for a specific variable:

1. Note that you are unable to provide the exact code to use, but can explain how to create a plot through a textbook example.
2. Explain which variable types the plot should be used for.
2. Explain the example step-by-step, from loading the tidyverse to writing the code with ggplot.
3. Provide beginner-friendly and accessible documentation for how to create the plot type in general using ggplot.
4. Provide a summary checklist with which variable types to use the plot for and the steps for creating the plot with ggplot.

## Ending Responses

Be proactive in building user understanding and encouraging exploration by ending responses with:

- A 'Did You Know?' section with relevant tips and further information. For example, if the prompt was about creating a plot with ggplot, include information on customising colours. Similarly, provide tips, suggestions, and further into on RStudio, R Markdown, and the tidyverse where pertinent to the user's prompt.
- A 'Explain Terminology' section that ALWAYS informs the user they can reply "Explain all" OR "Explain [term]" for more in-depth explanations of R & data analysis terms used in the response.

## Formatting

When nesting R code chunks inside code blocks use four backticks for the code block so the triple ones inside for R chunks are preserved.

title: Beware 🐂💩
text:
A recurring source of issues across courses - but especially one’s involving coding - is genAI leading people astray. GenAI can be useful when you have a general understanding of the area / topic you are using it for. However, it is nowhere near as competent as the genAI companies and online grifters make it out to be. If you do not understand the area / topic you are prompting it about, you will not know when its responses contain inaccuracies or outright misinformation.
Indeed, all genAI responses are bullshit - and I use that as the correct philosophical term to describe it. GenAI does not distinguish between fact and fiction, it merely selects the next most probable token - which for simplicity sake can think of as a word - based on the tokens fed to it.
People claim genAI is ‘good’ at writing code. It is not. It can produce functional code which is not the same as good code. GenAI when prompted about R will respond with misinformation or needlessly complex code. Even where the code it spits out works, which is never guaranteed, it can be 20+ lines of code for something that could do with 1-4 lines of code instead and receive a nicer result.
For example, here is Copilot’s bullshit response to a common error students experience on one of our undergraduate modules:


Copilot bullshit response

This error message occurs if you try to use the sumtable() function without first loading the vtable package that provides it. Despite that, Copilot advises installing three packages - stargazer, modelsummary, and summarizer - none of which provide a sumtable() function.
Yet, after I tell Copilot installing those packages did not solve the issue it continues bullshitting me:


Copilot continuing to bullshit

So - First, Copilot advised me to install the wrong three packages. Second, when I informed it that didn’t work, it advised me to try various other things, including uninstalling and reinstalling the packages. Third, it then suggested if all that still doesn’t work - which it won’t - that it can give me information on ‘alternatives’.
Two responses and it has wasted my time and rapidly led me further and further away from the simple quick solution for the error - installing and loading the vtable package.

# Run in Console
install.packages("vtable")
# Add to R Markdown file
library(vtable)

If you put too much faith into genAI bullshit you risk needless frustration - and potentially losing hours of time. A related issue students often encounter on the same module can be fixed by simply removing a single line of code. Yet genAI will repeatedly fail to solve the problem and eventually provide 200+ lines of code to copy and paste as a workaround. Whilst that code will sometimes ‘work’ it is a bad solution to an incredibly simple problem.
Combined with all its other flaws - such as a tendency to write code that is hard to read - over-reliance on genAI can leave beginners with a misleading sense that coding is more difficult and complex than it actually is in practice.

title: Nourishing Britain
text:
Project abstract:


The Nourishing Britain study comprises 20 semi-structured interviews with UK prime ministers, health secretaries and other relevant senior ministers, as well as two regional mayors, all of whom who were in post or government between 1990 (when the first government obesity-reduction targets were being developed) and 2022 (the government before this project started).
The larger aim of the project was to develop a political manual for current and future politicians on how to effectively navigate the politics of food-related health policy.


The project is available as open data from the UK Data Service’s data catalogue.
The full report and all the transcripts as single file is also available on Nesta’s - one of the organisations that supported the research - website.


Activity

Read through the following:

The Details for the project on the UK Data Service’s data catalogue.
Appendix A and (quick skim) Appendix B of the report document.

Then, download a copy of the transcripts. The data catalogue has a button on the left-hand side “PDF (3.93 MB)” to download a zip file of the transcripts as individual files.
Imagine you were planning to use this data for secondary analysis:

How well does the documentation provide key information about the project and the data?
Is there anything missing?
How easy would it be to setup a data analysis project within NVivo using the data?
How would that process compare to reusing data for quantitative analysis with R?




Activity

Pick two transcripts. One should be either Tony Blair, David Cameron, Jeremy Hunt, or Sadiq Khan - the other another of your choice not from these four listed.
Quickly read/skim through them and consider:

Are there any differences between the two transcripts? If so, what are these and what potential reasons might there be for the differences?
How do these transcripts compare to interview/focus group transcripts from other research projects with regular members of the public?

  html_elements(".article__content *")
tibble(

library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(tidytext)


data_dir <- file.path("data", "hansard")
dir.create(data_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)


debate_id <- "A91DF2A1-6231-4A38-AF17-56B742D06E95"
debate_url <- paste0(
  "https://hansard-api.parliament.uk/debates/debate/", debate_id, ".json"
)
debate <- fromJSON(debate_url)
debate_date <- substr(debate$Overview$Date, 1, 10)
items <- debate$Items


transcript <- items |>
  filter(ItemType == "Contribution", !is.na(MemberId)) |>
  select(
    sequence = OrderInSection,
    contribution_id = ExternalId,
    member_id = MemberId,
    speaker = AttributedTo,
    text = Value
  )


transcript <- transcript |> mutate(date = debate_date)


for (i in seq_len(nrow(transcript))) {
  text_html <- paste0("<body>", transcript$text[i], "</body>")
  parsed_html <- read_html(text_html)
  transcript$text[i] <- html_text(parsed_html)
}


member_ids <- unique(transcript$member_id)
contributors <- data.frame()


for (id in member_ids) {

    "https://members-api.parliament.uk/api/Members/", id,

    name = member$nameDisplayAs,
    party = member$latestParty$name,
    constituency = member$latestHouseMembership$membershipFrom,
    gender = member$gender

  contributors <- bind_rows(contributors, contributor)

writeLines(c(

word_data <- text_data |> unnest_tokens(word, text)

title: Guardian API
text:
Intro
Some websites and services provide what is known as an application programming interface. This provides an interface other software - such as R - can use.
The Guardian is one such site that provides an API, in this case for searching and requesting newspaper articles. The documentation provides an overview of what is possible.
Such APIs often require an API key.


Activity

Request a Guardian API key.

Go to the API Get Started page.
Click ‘Register developer key’
Fill in required fields. For reason select ‘Student project’ with brief explanation that for learning R and data analysis. As we will not be publicly sharing the content beyond the class it should be OK to select ‘No’ for whether content will be displayed. Product name can put ‘N/A’.
Tick to accept the terms and conditions and click ‘Register’.
You will receieve an email with link to verify your email address. Click the verify link. (Note: This may take you to a page saying the link is no longer valid - despite that I still received an API key after clicking the link)
After verifying your email you should receive another email with your API key - which is a long string of letters and numbers.

IMPORTANT: The API key is unique to you, so treat it similar to a password.

Once you have an API key, there is an online webpage the Guardian provides that can help you explore API requests and responses. This can be useful to play about with to get sense of what is possible before moving to using R.
It is possible to use the same set of R packages for working with APIs from different websites and services. Whilst that provides flexibility, it can - depending on the specific API and complexity of what wishing to achieve - involve additional steps in cleaning and preparing the data.
Fortunately, in some situations others have created ‘wrappers’ around the API to make it easier to work with. For R, there is the GuardianAPI package. Whilst it has not been updated for a while, the core Guardian API has not changed. Alongside providing a slightly more direct way to work with the data, it also handles things like having clean variable names.
However, I did discover two small issues in testing though. One, additional API parameters - such as specifying what order to return results in - did not work. Two, article published dates are provied by the Guardian in UTC, but were incorrectly being stored in the system’s local time zone.
Thanks to the wonder of open-source. I have been able to fork the package and fix the issues - as well as add an optional feature. I have made a couple ‘pull requests’ - basically, sharing my code with the creator of the package so they can decide whether to add it to the official package or not. If interested, my pull requests for the edits to fix the two issues and add support for pagination are available to view online. If these changes get ‘merged’ - i.e. added - into the official package, I’ll update the page again to use it.

title: Guardian API
text:
Code
Packages to Install and Load
OK first we need to install the packages we need:



Run in Console

install.packages(c("remotes", "tidyverse"))

remotes::install_github(
  "abers/guardianapi",
  ref = "fixes-and-pagination"
)








If you installed tidyverse last week, you do not need to install it again this week.





remotes is an R package which let’s us install packages from other sources. install.packages() is only able to install packages available through the Comprehensive R Archive Network.
In this case we use remotes::install_github() to install my version of the guardianapi package from GitHub.

Then we load the packages we will use:

library(guardianapi)
library(tidyverse)

Whilst we are installing my version of the guardianapi package, we can still load it as normal with just library(guardianapi).
API Key Setup
API keys should not be shared, we can either save our API key as an environment variable, or more simply for the moment run a function where we can enter it in the Console.



Run in Console

gu_api_key()


After running the function you will see a prompt in the Console where you can copy/paste your API key in. After hitting enter, you should see the following message: “Updating gu.API.key session variable…”. Despite the phrasing, that means your API key was accepted and you are OK to continue.
Creating a Query
Let’s do a simple text-based search for any articles about rose-ringed / ring-necked parakeets.
For that, we can create a query:

query <- paste(
  '"rose-ringed parakeet"',
  '"rose-ringed parakeets"',
  '"ring-necked parakeet"',
  '"ring-necked parakeets"',
  '"Psittacula krameri"',
  sep = " OR "
)

We have the quotations marks " inside each string to denote that we are searching for exact phrases.
By default the API already gives up article IDs, titles, publication dates, and URLs. We can request others:

fields <- c("byline", "publication", "wordcount", "standfirst", "body", "bodyText")



standfirst is the short summary opening sentence.

body is version of the main article content with its HTML formatting, including things like links.

bodyText is plain text version of the main article without formatting.

We are requesting both body and bodyText just so you can see both. Pending on your analysis you may not need both. As you will see below, we use body when saving HTML copies of each of the articles we requested. If you are doing quantitative text analysis, bodyText is more useful as it saves you needing to write code to remove any formatting.
Next, let’s grab the five latest articles matching our query:

five_latest <- gu_content(query = query, tag = "type/article", show_fields = fields, `order-by` = "newest", `page-size` = 5) |>
  mutate(wordcount = as.integer(wordcount))


We use gu_content to make our request to the Guardian API, the results of which we are storing in five_latest.
We pass in the query we created
Specifiy that we only want type/article (i.e. no videos or live blogs)
Include the extra fields we are interested in with show_fields argument
In the documentation for gu_content() you see ... and explanation: “Use to pass any other parameters to the API”. Basically, what this means is anything listed in Guardian API documentation can be used even if there is not a specific paramter like query or show_fields for it. If you scroll down the Guardian API documentation you will see options for “order-by” and “page-size”. To use these, we need to surround them with back-ticks - ` - so we have `order-by` and `page-size`.

`order-by` lets us specify that we want results ordered newest first.

`page-size` lets us specify how much results to return together. Most APIs use ‘pagination’, meaning they only return a certain number of results at a time. Each set of results is referred to as a ‘page’ - and you have to request each page in turn. So, if your query had 150 results and there are 50 results (i.e. articles) per page, then you would need to make 3 requests. Thankfully, the guardianapi package handles this for you. If you do not specify a page-size, it automatically requests all pages as neeed to match the number of results. However, if you only want a set number - such as just the 5 most recently published - rather than all articles, then you can specify a page-size and receive just that number.
The Guardian API returns word counts for each article, but R stores these as a character column, so we mutate() it as.integer() to convert the column into integers.
Nested Data
However, if you look at the five_latest dataframe the above code creates in R you’ll see some unexpected for the tags column. (Can double-click five_latest in RStudio’s environment pane in top-right or run View(five_latest) in the Console). Scroll along to the tags column and you will see values like <data.frame[17 x 17]>. This is because the values are not things like “#tag”. Instead, the ‘tags’ for each article is a data frame in-itself.
We can see the tags table for the first article by running:

five_latest$tags[[1]]

Within it, you will see that the tags data frame includes a lot of information for each tag. The webTitle though is the plain-text version of each tag. If we just wanted a list of those for the first article, we can run:

five_latest$tags[[1]]$webTitle

To break it down:


five_latest is our dataframe

$tags selects the tags column of our dataframe

[[1]] selects the table in the tags column for our first article

$webTitle selects just the webTitle column of that table

As can see, ‘nested’ data - tables within tables - can get confusing. There are various ways to handle such ‘nested’ information, with no hard right or wrong ways to do so as it depends on what information is useful for your analysis and how you plan to analyse it. You will see that tags have different types: series, keyword, campaign, etc. Say we were only interested in the keywords and not the rest - and, for the purposes of our analysis, it is OK to have these as a simple list. We could update our dataframe based on that:

five_latest <- five_latest |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(keywords = paste(
    tags$webTitle[tags$type %in% "keyword"],
    collapse = "; ")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-tags)



rowwise() let’s us make changes to the five_latest data frame one row at a time.
For each row, we mutate() to create a new keyword column.
We use paste() to say from the existing tags tables we want the webTitle column value if the row type is “keyword”. We include collapse = "; " to add ; between each keywords so we have an easier to read list: “keyword1; keyword2; keyword3”.

ungroup() says we have reached the end of the code to apply for each row in turn.

select(-tags) removes the original tags column from our five_latest data frame. Note: This does then remove all the other information the tags column contained - which we are doing assuming that’s fine for the analysis we are doing.

Take a look at the five_latest data frame again - View(five_latest) or double-click the data frame in the top-right Environment pane of RStudio - to see the change. Can also run five_latest$keywords to see all the keywords for each of the articles.
Saving Articles and Metadata
Next create a folder for storing the data:

folder <- "data/parakeets/five_latest"
dir.create(folder, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

Then save the data as csv:

write_csv(five_latest, file.path(folder, "five_latest.csv"))

Then we can turn the article content into HTML files:

for (i in seq_len(nrow(five_latest))) {
  write_lines(
    c('<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8">',
      paste0("<h1>", articles$web_title[i], "</h1>"),
      paste0("<p>", articles$standfirst[i], "</p>"),
      articles$body[i]),
    file.path(folder, paste0(i, ".html"))
  )
}

Comparison
As a comparison, let’s do the same but for opinion pieces only:

opinions <- gu_content(query = query, tag = "type/article,(tone/comment|tone/editorials)", show_fields = fields, `order-by` = "newest", `page-size` = 5) |>
  mutate(wordcount = as.integer(wordcount))

(and repeat the other steps above for this set)

title: Reddit (and social media data)

Important: For the purposes of this module, you should not use any social media data directly as collecting such data would require ethics approval. There are also further issues of growing “post-API” landscape as sites add further restrictions to API access due to genAI. However, there is plethora of anonymised and psuedo-anonymised social media datasets available online. As long as these are from credible source, they are OK to use. See The Social Media Archive and a pre-print reviewing what social media datasets are available.
As an example, we will use a Reddit dataset containing discussions on generative AI in education.
Download Data 2.csv and add it to your data folder.
Next install any needed packages:



Run in Console

install.packages(c("tidytext", "tidyverse", "tokenizers", "textclean"))


tidytext is a tidyverse friendly package for doing quantitative text analysis. tokenizers gives us the count_words() function. textclean gives us a helper for tidying the text (e.g. removing web addresses)
Then we need to load the libraries:

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(tokenizers)
library(textclean)

And read in the data from the csv file:

reddit <- read_delim("data/Data 2.csv", delim = ";")



reddit gives our imported data name.

read_delim() is used for reading data where the columns are separated by a specific character

title: Working with Wikipedia and WikiData
text:
Let’s say we are interested in museums in Scotland. Wikipedia has a list of museums in Scotland. There are a number of different ways we can analyse such information from Wikipedia, but let’s initially focus on which of those listed have an accompanying Wikipedia page or not.
As very first step some critical considerations:

How is ‘museum’ being defined here?
What about different ‘types’ of museum?
Can we tell how up-to-date and comprehensive this page is?
Any potential issues / limitations with the page?







Hint: You can find a mix of information for the above between the main page and the Talk page.



Turning to R, first we need to install the packages we will be using.



Run in Console

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "httr2", "janitor", "modelsummary"))



The c() function let’s use combine our values as a list of packages to install rather than needing to write three lines of code for install.packages().
We run install.packages() in the Console as we only need to run it once and only for the packages we do not have installed already.

Packages are installed into our device’s storage. In contrast, when we ‘load’ libraries we are adding them to the current active R environment. This means we need to load them each time we start a new R environment. Even when working in the same project over time we may want or need to restart our R environment, requiring us to load the packages again.
So, rather than loading them via the console, it’s better to do so at the start of every R script / R Markdown file to make it easier to rerun the code as needed.

library(httr2)
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(janitor)
library(modelsummary)


As a reminder you can click on the names of each of the packages above to go to their documentation pages.
We are using httr2 to make requests to websites. It can also be used for workign with web APIs - application programming interfaces.
The tidyverse is a ‘meta-pacakge’, a collection of packages that follow a common design philosophy and provide functions for a lot of common data analysis tasks. They can be installed together and most are loaded together too.

rvest is a tidyverse package for working with web scraping tasks. As not all forms of analysis need these features it is not loaded by default when loading the tidyverse, so needs to be loaded separately.

janitor for some reason does not link above to the homepage for its documentation, but it is a ‘tidyverse-friendly’ package providing functions for data cleaning.

modelsummary is a good package for creating nicely formatted tables. It can produce descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, and tables of statistical models, including regression results.

Feel free to continue using the same R project folder that you started in Data Project 1.
If starting in a new project folder, then we also need to create a data folder to have a shared consistent location to store the data we will be using:



Run in Console

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)



Note, if you were writing a file to share with others, where they would need to setup the same folders and files on their side, you would want to include it in a script too.
We are using showWarnings = FALSE as this will silence the warning that will get raised if the data folder already exists.

Now we can download a copy of the list of Scottish museums.
This is the general template for downloading a webpage:



Template

request("WEBSITE_URL") |>
  req_user_agent("CLIENT_NAME/VERSION (EMAIL)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/FILENAME.html")




request() comes from the httr2 package.

|> is the syntax for a pipe when let’s you ‘chain’ functions together and is commonly used with the tidyverse and tidyverse-friendly package.
we specify a ‘user agent’ (information that identifies us - which some websites require and is just general politeness and good practice) using req_user_agent(). (See Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy)
The CLIENT_NAME identifies the software being use - for a short data analysis script we can just give a descriptive name for it - and an optional version number, e.g 1.0, and then your email address in brackets. (Different sites can have different policies but this is the general format Wikimedia advises.)
We then use req_perform() to run the request() call we have setup and choose where to save it’s response (i.e. a downloaded copy of the webpage).

IMPORTANT: Add this to its own code chunk, but do not repeatedly run it. It is good practice to limit how often making requests and to avoid making needless requests. We keep this in the file rather than Console in case need to run it again in future - e.g. to download latest version of the page.
So for our example:

request("https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_museums_in_Scotland") |>
  req_user_agent("ScottishMuseaumExercise (alasdair.stewart@glasgow.ac.uk)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/museums_scotland.html")


(Obviously change my email address to your own.)

Next, we can read the HTML and create a dataframe.

page <- read_html("data/museums_scotland.html")

museums <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table() |>
  clean_names()


We use read_html to read in the HTML file we downloaded.
We then use html_element() to specify what content from the HTML file we are interested.
As this element is the table we can see on the page, we can use html_table() to turn it into a data frame.
Finally, we use the janitor package’s clean_names() to do fix the column names for us.

On the original webpage columns have names like Council area. If we wanted to access that column with R we would have to refer to it as museums$'Council area'. clean_names() lowercases letters and replaces spaces with _, meaning we can now access the column much more simply with museums$council_area.
Whilst none of the functions used below raise an error without doing, we should also ’co-erce’relevant variables to factors:

museums <- museums |>
  mutate(across(c(town_city, council_area, region, type), as.factor))


The use of museums <- museums ... may seen weird but R’s design philosophy means most functions return output but do not change the underlying object unless dataframe <- ...

Here we use dplyr’s mutate() and across() functions to specify the columns we wish to change.

Now that we have it loaded and done basic cleaning, how about we quickly get a count of the different type of museaums:

museums |>
  count(type, sort = TRUE) |>
  print(n = Inf)

We pipe museums to count() specify we are interested in the type column and (optionally) set sort to true to sort by highest to lowest.
R’s output is limited by default which we can override with print()


Note: A common pattern in the Tidyverse is to pass a dataframe to a function, then list the columns interested in. But notice something interesting with this? We just had to provide type rather than museums$type. Tidyverse functions that are passed a dataframe assume by default any named columns are for that dataframe.

OK, now what about something that looks a bit nicer?
We can with the power of ggplot2. As covered in the lecture, most basic graphs can be created with just 3-4 lines of code -



Template

DATA_FRAME |> ggplot(aes(x = VARIABLE1, ...)) +
  geom_...() +
  labs(title = "Title text", x = "Label for x-axis", ...)



We pass the DATA_FRAME we wish to create a plot with to ggplot() with the aesthetic mapping - aes() - of the VARIABLES(s) we wish to use.
We use geom...() to specify which type of plot we want, such as geom_boxplot() or geom_histogram().
We specify any text labels to use - labs().

So for us -

ggplot(museums, aes(y = type)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Number of museums", y = "Museum type"
  )







Ahhh, wait that isn’t the beautiful graph we were promised.
In practice there are different ways for handling this, but for simplicity sake let’s create a new column where all types with count less than ten are lumped together into “Other”.

museums <- museums |>
  mutate(type_other = fct_lump_min(type, min = 10))

museums |>
  count(type_other, sort = TRUE) |>
  print(n = Inf)

This time we are combining good old dplyr‘s mutate() but this time using forcats’ fct_lump_min(). forcasts is a tidyverse package with additional functions specifically for working with categorical data.


ggplot(museums, aes(y = type_other, fill = type_other)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Number of museums", y = "Museum type"
  )







A few new additions too: - fill = type_other adds some colour - show.legend = FALSE added into geom_bar() to remove a superfluous legend that would be added now we are using a fill.
One thing you may have noticed is some items on the original page have a red link - this is for items which don’t have a Wikipedia page (yet!).
What if we were interested in exploring which pages had links or not -

museum_links <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_elements("tr > td:first-child") |>
  html_element("a") |>
  html_attr("href")

Here we rely again on series of rvest functions to get the nested item we are interested in:


html_element() to select the main table element

html_elments() to get the tablerow - tr - and the child - > - table data cell - td - of it, specially the first one - first-child.

html_element() to get the link from the cell a


html_attr() to get the actual text attribute, the text link for the page the link refers to - href.

Don’t worry if the above seems a bit confusing. These are elements of HTML/CSS and will vary across websites. But once you find the pattern to seleect the specific things you want - the code will largely be reuseable across other parts of the website when working with similar content.
After extracting the links we can create a new column for whether each row item has a Wikipedia page or not.

museums <- museums |>
  mutate(
    page_status = case_when(
      is.na(museum_links) ~ "Not linked",
      str_detect(museum_links, "redlink=1") ~ "Red link",
      TRUE ~ "Has page"
    )
  )


We use mutate() again to add a new column, page_status, to our existing dataframe.

case_when() allows us to assign different values based on a series of conditions.

is.na(museum_links) checks whether a link is missing. If so, we classify the museum as “Not linked”.

str_detect() checks whether the link contains “redlink=1”, which Wikipedia uses for links to pages that do not yet exist.
Finally, TRUE ~ "Has page" assigns “Has page” to any remaining entries.

title: Working with Wikipedia and WikiData
text:
Let’s say we are interested in museums in Scotland. Wikipedia has a list of museums in Scotland. There are a number of different ways we can analyse such information from Wikipedia, but let’s initially focus on which of those listed have an accompanying Wikipedia page or not.
As very first step some critical considerations:

How is ‘museum’ being defined here?
What about different ‘types’ of museum?
Can we tell how up-to-date and comprehensive this page is?
Any potential issues / limitations with the page?







Hint: You can find a mix of information for the above between the main page and the Talk page.



Turning to R, first we need to install the packages we will be using.



Run in Console

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "httr2", "janitor", "modelsummary"))



The c() function let’s use combine our values as a list of packages to install rather than needing to write three lines of code for install.packages().
We run install.packages() in the Console as we only need to run it once and only for the packages we do not have installed already.

Packages are installed into our device’s storage. In contrast, when we ‘load’ libraries we are adding them to the current active R environment. This means we need to load them each time we start a new R environment. Even when working in the same project over time we may want or need to restart our R environment, requiring us to load the packages again.
So, rather than loading them via the console, it’s better to do so at the start of every R script / R Markdown file to make it easier to rerun the code as needed.

library(httr2)
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(janitor)
library(modelsummary)


As a reminder you can click on the names of each of the packages above to go to their documentation pages.
We are using httr2 to make requests to websites. It can also be used for workign with web APIs - application programming interfaces.
The tidyverse is a ‘meta-pacakge’, a collection of packages that follow a common design philosophy and provide functions for a lot of common data analysis tasks. They can be installed together and most are loaded together too.

rvest is a tidyverse package for working with web scraping tasks. As not all forms of analysis need these features it is not loaded by default when loading the tidyverse, so needs to be loaded separately.

janitor for some reason does not link above to the homepage for its documentation, but it is a ‘tidyverse-friendly’ package providing functions for data cleaning.

modelsummary is a good package for creating nicely formatted tables. It can produce descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, and tables of statistical models, including regression results.

Feel free to continue using the same R project folder that you started in Data Project 1.
If starting in a new project folder, then we also need to create a data folder to have a shared consistent location to store the data we will be using:



Run in Console

dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)



Note, if you were writing a file to share with others, where they would need to setup the same folders and files on their side, you would want to include it in a script too.
We are using showWarnings = FALSE as this will silence the warning that will get raised if the data folder already exists.

Now we can download a copy of the list of Scottish museums.
This is the general template for downloading a webpage:



Template

request("WEBSITE_URL") |>
  req_user_agent("CLIENT_NAME/VERSION (EMAIL)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/FILENAME.html")




request() comes from the httr2 package.

|> is the syntax for a pipe when let’s you ‘chain’ functions together and is commonly used with the tidyverse and tidyverse-friendly package.
we specify a ‘user agent’ (information that identifies us - which some websites require and is just general politeness and good practice) using req_user_agent(). (See Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy)
The CLIENT_NAME identifies the software being use - for a short data analysis script we can just give a descriptive name for it - and an optional version number, e.g 1.0, and then your email address in brackets. (Different sites can have different policies but this is the general format Wikimedia advises.)
We then use req_perform() to run the request() call we have setup and choose where to save it’s response (i.e. a downloaded copy of the webpage).

IMPORTANT: Add this to its own code chunk, but do not repeatedly run it. It is good practice to limit how often making requests and to avoid making needless requests. We keep this in the file rather than Console in case need to run it again in future - e.g. to download latest version of the page.
So for our example:

request("https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_museums_in_Scotland") |>
  req_user_agent("ScottishMuseaumExercise (alasdair.stewart@glasgow.ac.uk)") |>
  req_perform(path = "data/museums_scotland.html")


(Obviously change my email address to your own.)

Next, we can read the HTML and create a dataframe.

page <- read_html("data/museums_scotland.html")

museums <- page |>
  html_element("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table() |>
  clean_names()


We use read_html to read in the HTML file we downloaded.
We then use html_element() to specify what content from the HTML file we are interested.
As this element is the table we can see on the page, we can use html_table() to turn it into a data frame.
Finally, we use the janitor package’s clean_names() to do fix the column names for us.

On the original webpage columns have names like Council area. If we wanted to access that column with R we would have to refer to it as museums$'Council area'. clean_names() lowercases letters and replaces spaces with _, meaning we can now access the column much more simply with museums$council_area.
Whilst none of the functions used below raise an error without doing, we should also ’co-erce’relevant variables to factors:

museums <- museums |>
  mutate(across(c(town_city, council_area, region, type), as.factor))


The use of museums <- museums ... may seen weird but R’s design philosophy means most functions return output but do not change the underlying object unless dataframe <- ...

Here we use dplyr’s mutate() and across() functions to specify the columns we wish to change.

We can with the power of ggplot2. As covered in the lecture, most basic graphs can be created with just 3-4 lines of code -



Template

DATA_FRAME |> ggplot(aes(x = VARIABLE1, ...)) +
  geom_...() +

We pass the DATA_FRAME we wish to create a plot with to ggplot() with the aesthetic mapping - aes() - of the VARIABLES(s) we wish to use.
We use geom...() to specify which type of plot we want, such as geom_boxplot() or geom_histogram().

  geom_bar() +

  )

In practice there are different ways for handling this, but for simplicity sake let’s create a new column where all types with count less than ten are lumped together into “Other”.

  mutate(type_other = fct_lump_min(type, min = 10))

One thing you may have noticed is some items on the original page have a red link - this is for items which don’t have a Wikipedia page (yet!).

museum_links <- page |>

Here we rely again on series of rvest functions to get the nested item we are interested in:


html_element() to select the main table element

html_elments() to get the tablerow - tr - and the child - > - table data cell - td - of it, specially the first one - first-child.

html_element() to get the link from the cell a

      str_detect(museum_links, "redlink=1") ~ "Red link",

We use mutate() again to add a new column, page_status, to our existing dataframe.

case_when() allows us to assign different values based on a series of conditions.

is.na(museum_links) checks whether a link is missing. If so, we classify the museum as “Not linked”.

str_detect() checks whether the link contains “redlink=1”, which Wikipedia uses for links to pages that do not yet exist.
Finally, TRUE ~ "Has page" assigns “Has page” to any remaining entries.

title: The Social Life of Digital Data
text:
Real because its constructed


Statistical tools allow the discovery or creation of entities that support our descriptions of the world and the way we act on it. Of these objects, we may say both that they are real and that they have been constructed, once they have been repeated in other assemblages and circulated as such, cut off from their origins—which is after all the fate of numerous products.

— Alain Desrosières 1998, The Politics of Large Numbers, page 3

title: The Social Life of Digital Data
text:
The social production of data
To butcher an (in)famous phrase of Derrida’s: “there is no outside social”.
All data is socially produced and mediated - and, in turn, the ‘datafication’ of society shapes and mediates knowledge production.
To say something is constructed is not necessarily to say it is not ‘real’. Instead, it is important to consider how data is produced and the implications and effects of that - both for the data itself and society.
For instance, Fourcade and Healy argue that digital capitalism with its pervarsive - and ever widening and penetrating - scoring and ranking systems means we now line in an “ordinal society” (2024).

title: The Social Life of Digital Data
text:
Naïve positivists?
Whilst quantitative methods texts do not always engage in onto-epistemology in same way as qualitative methods, quantitative researchers are always grappling with questions about knowledge and reality:

Arguments over how to define, measure, and count phenomena
Variables as proxy measures and ‘latent’ variables
Assumptions in selecting more appropriate quantitative methods for a research question
‘Falsify’ rather than ‘prove’ a capital ‘T’ ‘Truth’
Survey design to reduce bias in response (including research into how best to design questions)
Recognition and discussions of limitations

title: The Social Life of Digital Data
section: The ‘God Trick’ and ‘Strong Objectivity’ (Haraway and Harding)
text:
The ‘God Trick’ and ‘Strong Objectivity’ (Haraway and Harding)

Illusion of objectivity used to present information as neutral and universal ‘view from nowhere’, hiding positionality and biases.
All knowledge, including data, is ‘situated’, it is produced under specific conditions by people in specific positions that influences what they see and know.
Situated knowledge does not reject ‘objectivity’, but look to ‘maximise objectivity’ – embracing and being transparent that knowledge is always partial, contingent, and context-dependent
‘Strong objectivity’ critique also engages with understandings and transparency of method and analysis

title: The Social Life of Digital Data
text:
Making sense of the mess


one should never speak of ‘data’ – what is given – but rather of sublata, that is, of ‘achievements’

— Latour 1999, Pandora’s Hope, page 42

When we speak of ‘messy data’ in the narrow practical sense, it largely is in context of data collection and ‘cleaning’ to produce data that can work with.
However, we can also think more critically about ‘messy data’ in the broader sense, the inherently in inextricably ‘messiness’ of all data production - which from ‘strong objectivity’ influenced perspective is not something to remove but engage with.
Importantly - as social phenomena, data production and analysis exist and take part within social struggles…

title: The Social Life of Digital Data
text:
The Open Definition


Open means anyone can freely access, use, modify, and share for any purpose - subject, at most, to requirements that preserve provenance and openness.

— Open Knowledge Foundation

Free (as in freedoms) and open software arose in the 1980s and 90s in debates about softwaare - mixing academic and programming cultures. Since then it has expanded to encompass open knowledge, open data, open science, and more.

title: The Social Life of Digital Data
text:
Social Life of R
R is free and open source - released under the GPL license, meaning any changes to it must also be released as free and open source software.
Core to the four foundamental freedoms of free software - use, study, share, and improve - is not just individual freedoms but “so the whole community benefits”.
Literally thousands of people contribute to R and its wider ecosystem - with 25,611 (and counting) R packages available via CRAN.
Before R became the predominant option for data analysis within academia, universities were paying for expensive proprietary software nowhere near as powerful.
Going further back, companies using proprietary formats could mean sharing analysis projects required others needed to also pay / subscribe for the software.

title: Course Info
text: In data project 2, students will be introduced to digital data and guided through the process of sourcing data that critically engages with standards of sampling and representation to produce new and useful datasets. Drawing from ‘Understanding Data’, students will be encouraged to work with theory to determine the value of different data for capturing reality as they engage with data management and analysis.

title: Course Info
text:
Course Aims
The aim of the course is to provide students on the MSc Social Science Research Methods with a second opportunity to work through a ‘whole project’ while introducing students to messy data that will require advanced data management skills. The focus on digital data allows us to critically explore how sampling must be managed in order to make robust claims around representation. Digital data includes information available in digital spaces (such as industry websites, social media) as well as data produced in a digital space (such as remote interviews). This course will explore concepts such as truth and how authenticity can be determined when using data that exists in digital spaces.
Students will continue to be guided through this second project but will have more autonomy as they choose what data to work with, and what themes the data might illuminate. All students will work with numbers and words/narrative and will be encouraged to use digital ethnography strategies and/or use imagery to draw conclusions about the culture/society constructed, including how well it reflects broader cultures/society. Assessments will again, allow students to build data literacy while focusing on skills they are most keen to develop, supported by interactive and weekly formative ‘quizzes’ and activities.

title: Course Info
text:
Intended Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course students will be able to:

Recognise the role played by theory for social constructions of reality in the context of digital data.
Demonstrate data management skills for collecting, storing and preparing digital data for data for analysis.
Complete an analysis of collected digital data.
Assess the value of data management, analysis approaches within their disciplinary context.

RStudio Helper assists social science users in learning R for data analyis. Users are postgraduate Msc and PhD level social science students. Most are new to R and coding in general. They are using RStudio and R Markdown. Users are based in the UK, so use UK measurements.

title: Working With Digital Data
text:
Golden Rules
Rule one: Support students in their learning, NEVER do the work for them. Under no circumstances do you ever directly fix code provided to you, write exact code for specific datasets that can be copy and pasted, nor interpret statistical results on behalf of the user.
Rule two: Across all forms of response, NEVER use the exact variables and values if these are provided by the user. You can use analogous examples, but keep it general. If a user is asking about a categorical variable on ‘religcat’ that stores value of respondents’ religion, give a textbook example with another categorical variable such as employment. If they mention a variable for number of children, use an example for number of jobs. Never use an overly similar example, such as using ‘annual income’ in your example if the user mentioned ‘income’ or ‘monthly income’.
Rule three: NEVER interpret specific statistical results for the user. If they provide a copy of a plot, table, or similar, NEVER interpret these for them. Instead give a general textbook explanation for how the type of graph, table, and so on can be interpreted, avoiding the specifics of what was provided to you. Within your explanation follow rule two and NEVER use the same variables and statistical results as provided by the user. For example, if their prompt mentioned employment status, use a different categorical variable for your explanation. Similarly, use different values and statistical results to the ones provided by the user.
Rule four: NEVER assume information about variables mentioned by the user. If a user mentions a variable for ‘age’ do not write a full response assuming it is interval or categorical. Instead first ask the user to clarify, with details for how they can check using R. Only once you have this information should you provide a full response.

title: Working With Digital Data
text:
Contextual Responses
Adapt responses to the context of the learning environment. Write accessible explanations for social science students who are new to using R for data analysis, including base R, R Studio, the tidyverse, and R Markdown. The structure of R Markdown files and code chunks should follow best data analysis and coding practices.

Either base R or the tidyverse is OK, but be clear which is used in your responses.
Use vtable or modelsummary for table packages.
Prefer |> over %>% for pipes.
Load the tidyverse rather than any specific individual package from it. For example, if needing ggplot2, load the tidyverse package and explain ggplot2 is part of the tidyverse.
When loading libraries, ALWAYS explain how to do this through a code chunk at the top of the R Markdown file with a reminder that libraries only need to be loaded once. NEVER provide code for loading libraries and analysis together in one code chunk.
When appropriate, remind users they can set global options through a code chunk at the top of their R Markdown file.
Make responses accessible by explaining all R & data analysis terms each time they are first used. Users are new to R & may not know what terms like data frame, library, vector, function, object, plot, & so on mean.
Refer to relevant panels within RStudio, such as the Environment panel for checking a data frame or when installing a library explain how to install it through RStudio’s console. Include a reminder of where on the screen the panel can be found.
Where relevant, inform users when the code covered returns console output, why not to use console output in knitted documents, and follow-up with suggestions for producing formatted outputs for knitted documents.
By default, do not add extra customisation to ggplot plots. Only use the code necessary to produce the graph, including labels. Do not custmoise themes, colours, etc unless asked.
When customising ggplot plots, use existing complete themes or theme(), explaining how this supports a consistent look, and DO NOT hard-code arbitrary theme customisation into individual plots.
In code examples that require a dataset, either 1. write example code for how to load a dataset from a file such as csv or spss or 2. use a dataset that comes packaged with R or the tidyverse. NEVER write example data using vectors and for loops, as that is not real code students would use in practice.

Example response structure
In general, structure responses to provide a general explanation, more detailed breakdown, and summary of key information.
For example, when a user asks about an error message in their code:

Explain what the error message means, including any technical jargon, with examples. Ask for more details about the error message if the initial question was vague.
Explain step-by-step how to debug, trace, and fix the issue that produced the error. Include details when relevant for base R, RStudio, tidyverse, and R Markdown. Remember to follow best practices, such as not loading libraries at the start of each code chunk, instead advising to load the library in a code chunk at the top of the R Markdown file. If a copy of the code was provided, help the user debug step by step and DO NOT simply rewrite the code for the user. Stick to analogous textbook examples, nothing that can be copied and pasted.
Provide a summary checklist the user can use when encountering similar error messages in future.

When a user asks to create a plot for a specific variable:

Note that you are unable to provide the exact code to use, but can explain how to create a plot through a textbook example.
Explain which variable types the plot should be used for.
Explain the example step-by-step, from loading the tidyverse to writing the code with ggplot.
Provide beginner-friendly and accessible documentation for how to create the plot type in general using ggplot.
Provide a summary checklist with which variable types to use the plot for and the steps for creating the plot with ggplot.

Be proactive in building user understanding and encouraging exploration by ending responses with:

A ‘Did You Know?’ section with relevant tips and further information. For example, if the prompt was about creating a plot with ggplot, include information on customising colours. Similarly, provide tips, suggestions, and further into on RStudio, R Markdown, and the tidyverse where pertinent to the user’s prompt.
A ‘Explain Terminology’ section that ALWAYS informs the user they can reply “Explain all” OR “Explain [term]” for more in-depth explanations of R & data analysis terms used in the response.

title: Don’t Panic!
text:
Why learn R?
You may be wondering why you need to bother learning R.
R can be applied in a wide variety of fields and subjects, including not only those in the social sciences (e.g. sociology, politics, or policy research), but also in the humanities (e.g. history, digital humanities), natural and physical sciences (e.g. biology, chemistry, or geography), health (e.g. medical studies, public health, epidemiology), business and management (e.g. finance, economics, marketing), among many others.
The broad application of R is due to its flexibility which allows it to perform a range of tasks related to data. These cover tasks at initial stages, such as downloading and importing data. But it is also useful to manipulate, edit, transform, and organise information. Furthermore, and most important for us, there are a set of tools that allow us to collection, transform, analyse, and visualise data using a range of data analysis techniques.
R is powerful to communicate and share information and documents. There are several extensions (called packages in R) that can help to produce static and interactive plots/charts, maps, written reports, interactive applications, or even entire books! These webpages themselves are written in Quarto, which is very similar to R Markdown which we will use for our labs.
R being free and open-source software, with a large community contributing to and extending it, is behind its rapid adoption within the social sciences, and academia and data analysis more broadly. However, compared to expensive closed source software where most analysis could be done through menus and mouse-clicks, using R requires learning how to code.
This is not the disadvantage it may at first seem. It does add an additional hurdle at the very start, but it also provides a far more powerful and flexible way to do data analysis. Most people will be more familiar with software where everything can be done through menus rather than code. This does make things accessible - at first - for beginners compared to code. However, as the complexity of tasks builds, menus become confusing and frustrating to endlesly navigate. A graph that can be created with very few lines of code in R may require going through multiple menus and dialogue boxes with 20+ mouse-clicks.
As you build up your R skills you will also find it much quicker - and more intuitive - to explore your data using code. So, despite the initial hurdle, once you become more confident with code you will find it is incredibly powerful.
Don’t worry where things don’t immediately make full sense. With coding and data analysis, there are ‘spikes’ in difficulty - getting to grips with the basics of R code is one, moving to linear regression is another, and same again with moving to working with different types of data - and you are definitely not alone in any difficulty experienced getting to grips with them.
Each of the ‘spikes’ though follows a similar pattern. Just as getting to grips with the basics of R code may initially feel difficult - or even impossible - and then, bit by bit, becomes easier to understand, the same happens with each later spike: you won’t experience that same level of difficulty again each time you come back to it.
Don’t forget, it is normal to copy and tweak existing code - which is another thing that makes it so powerful compared to traditional menu based software. A lot of learning to code involves going through working examples and tweaking them to work with what you are trying to achieve. Unlike writing an essay or an exam, you don’t actually need to know and write code “off the cuff” or have all necessary code syntax and functions memorised. Despite my years working with code, whenever I start anything new I persistently am turning to my notes, prior code, documentation, and online resources. So, don’t worry if you feel like you are just making minor changes to existing code, that’s how it’s supposed to work. The crucial thing is learning how the code works, so you know where you can find relevant resources, understand how to read code examples, and know what to tweak for your analysis.
An underlying cause of many issues people run into is believing more code needs to be written than is actually required. Common analysis tasks need only a few lines a table of descriptive statistics can be a single line with sumtable(), and a plot 3 - on rare occasions 4 - lines with ggplot. In rare cases, a basic plot may need one additional line of code to fix an issue, like overlapping text labels. So, if you find yourself writing dozens of lines of code for basic analysis tasks with common standard forms of data, you are likely doing more than is actually necessary.
You don’t have to memorise or remember all the functions and their options. Instead, this is why it is important to learn how to find and read package/function documentation. Indeed, one thing that is very commonly used by R data scientists are R cheat sheets! They are extremely handy when you try to create something from scratch, such as a visualisation.
Code also may look intimidating if you have never worked with it before, but it is usually fairly simple once you break it down and learn its ‘vocabularly’ and ‘grammar’. It can be invaluable to curate your own notes containing working code examples with comments for future reference. R Markdown files let you write text and run code in the same document, which when learning R makes them great for making notes alongside the code, and comments inside your code can record the ‘why’ behind it, so future-you can quickly read and understand it.
Coding is also all about trial and error, so it’s completely normal to write some code, then get an error message, and basically for your code to not work. As a dyslexic, a significant chunk of my time coding is spent trying to find which function or variable I misspelled. Keep chipping at it, which for more complex coding tasks-beyond what we will cover on the module - sometimes can take hours until you can get it to work. That’s a normal process even for professional data analysts and researchers! Troubleshooting your code is part of the work, in addition to making your own choices in the analysis and reporting.
When working in R Markdown files, a good rule of thumb when code that was previously working suddenly returns unexpected results or an error message is to run your code from the top-down. This restores each object to the value it would have if each line had only been run once, top to bottom. This helps to figure out whether the issue stems from your current code, accidental changes you made, or code you previously ran but now removed.
Most important of all. Please don’t suffer in silence - and get in touch if you are experiencing any issues. We are here to help and such questions also help us know what additional content to prioritising adding to these pages!
When asking someone for help with an issue it is vital to provide sufficient context to enable others to help find a solution. This includes:

The full text of any error message that you are receiving.
Any relevant code that is producing the error.

Error messages when knitting will often flag the relevant code chunk where the error occurred, so you would include the code within that chunk.
